analysis.one_liner: Guarantees most workers 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave for births, adoptions, and family illness.
analysis.headline: The bill guaranteeing 12 weeks of job-protected family and medical leave never received a committee vote and died when the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have let employees at companies with 50 or more workers take up to 12 weeks of unpaid leave — with their job and health insurance protected — for a birth, an adoption, a family member's serious illness, or their own serious health condition [S2] [S3]. It would have extended the same rights to federal civil service employees and set up a commission to study the costs and effects of leave policies [S2] [S3]. Introduced in the last months of the 101st Congress, it never got a committee vote and died when that Congress ended [S1] [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Employees at employers with 50 or more workers who need time off for a birth, an adoption, a serious family illness, or their own serious health condition. They would keep their job (or an equivalent one) and their health insurance while on leave, and could sue or file a complaint with the Labor Department if an employer interfered or retaliated [S2] [S3]. Federal civil service employees would get the same protections under Title II [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Entitles eligible employees to 12 workweeks of unpaid, job-protected leave during any 12-month period for the birth or adoption of a child, to care for a child, spouse, or parent with a serious health condition, or for their own serious health condition.
Requires employers to maintain the employee's group health insurance during the leave and to restore the employee to the same or an equivalent position on return, with accrued benefits preserved.

Backs the right with real enforcement: workers can file charges with the Secretary of Labor or go to court, employers cannot retaliate against people who assert these rights, and violators owe lost wages plus additional damages and attorneys' fees.
Extends the same 12 weeks of family and temporary medical leave, job protection, and health-insurance continuation to federal civil service employees.

Spells out protections aimed at sex discrimination in caregiving: Congress found that women bear most family caretaking duties and that gender-neutral leave reduces employers' incentive to discriminate against women in hiring.

analysis.who_pays: Employers with 50 or more employees, who would have to hold jobs open for up to 12 weeks, keep paying health insurance premiums for workers on leave, and arrange coverage for absent employees; the bill's own commission on leave was tasked with studying the costs, benefits, and productivity impact on employers [S2] [S3]. Small businesses with fewer than 50 employees at a worksite were exempt [S2] [S3].

drawbacks.text: The leave is unpaid: the bill states it does not require an employer to provide paid sick or medical leave where it normally would not, so many workers — especially lower-wage ones — could not afford to take the time off the bill guarantees.

Coverage is narrow: employees at worksites where the employer has fewer than 50 people within 75 miles are excluded, and spouses working for the same employer can have their combined leave capped at 12 weeks for a birth, adoption, or care of a sick parent.

Employers bear real costs — holding positions open, maintaining health coverage, and covering for absent workers — which is why the bill created a Commission on Leave to study the impact on employers and whether to change coverage of small businesses.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — knowing you can care for a newborn or a seriously ill family member without losing your job or health insurance — is large and reaches millions of workers, while the compliance cost falls on a defined set of midsize and large employers and the bill is deliberately cautious (50-employee threshold, unpaid leave, employer-friendly certification and notice rules). The main design weakness is that unpaid leave helps workers who can afford to go without pay far more than those who cannot, and the smallest employers are left out entirely. On balance it is a real, if limited, gain for working people at a modest, targeted cost to employers.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in the closing months of the 101st Congress, it was sent to the Senate Labor Committee, never got a committee vote or a floor vote, and died when that Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Senator Christopher Dodd introduced the bill on August 3, 1990, joined from the start by a bipartisan list of 25 cosponsors, including Republicans Bob Packwood and Mark Hatfield.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources the same day.
No further action appears in the record: the committee never voted on it, the full Senate never debated it, and the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991, killing the bill.
The 25 cosponsors meant the bill carried real bipartisan support on paper — 23 of 55 Senate Democrats and 2 of 45 Senate Republicans — but that support never translated into a vote of any kind.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large employers were spared a new leave mandate for another two years. Workers got nothing from this bill; the same guarantee of 12 weeks of job-protected family and medical leave only became law in 1993, after a change in administration.

for.name: Christopher Dodd
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Family and Medical Leave Act of 1990 and recruited a bipartisan list of 25 original cosponsors.

for.name: Edward Kennedy
for.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill and was named in its introduction; the bill was referred to the committee he chaired, which never acted on it.

for.name: Bob Packwood and Mark Hatfield
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors, making the bill bipartisan from day one.

against.name: George H. W. Bush
against.what_they_did: Vetoed the House-passed family and medical leave bill (H.R. 770), the same proposal's House version, in June 1990, and the veto was sustained when a House override fell short — leaving this Senate bill as a late-session reintroduction that leadership did not advance.

sides.party_line_note: Support leaned heavily Democratic: 23 of 55 Senate Democrats cosponsored the bill versus 2 of 45 Senate Republicans, and the Senate never held a vote on it.

industries.note: These employers would have to hold jobs open for up to 12 weeks, maintain health coverage for workers on leave, and cover for absences — a direct compliance cost. Their interest in avoiding the mandate ran against the job security the bill promised workers.

industries.industry: Small businesses (fewer than 50 employees per worksite)
industries.note: The bill explicitly exempts worksites with fewer than 50 employees within 75 miles, so small businesses avoid the mandate entirely — but their employees get none of the leave rights, showing how the carve-out shifts the burden of exclusion onto workers.

industries.industry: Group health insurers and employer benefit plans
industries.note: By requiring employers to keep paying group health premiums for workers on leave, the bill keeps workers tied to employer-sponsored insurance rather than creating any alternative coverage; insurers keep the premium stream during the 12 weeks.
